summary: Describes a mechanism that puts version numbers on EID-to-RLOC mappings and carries them in the LISP header of encapsulated packets. This gives in-packet information about the mappings used and helps detect when they are out of date. It obsoletes RFC 6834. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Each address book entry gets a version number written on the envelope. If it is older than the newest one, the receiver knows to go ask for the update.

questions: how does lisp detect stale mappings
subtitle: Version numbers on LISP mappings let routers notice stale address mappings straight from the packet header.

tldr.problem: In LISP, routers cache mappings from endpoint IDs to routing locators, and a cached mapping can become out of date when the owner changes its locators, priorities or weights.
tldr.mechanism: Each mapping gets a 12-bit Map-Version number that is carried in the LISP header (source and destination versions) and in Map Records, so a receiving router can compare versions and send a Map-Request or drop the packet.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism is optional and ignored by routers that do not support it. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 6834 and must only be used in trusted, closed deployments.

today: RFC 9302 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the experimental RFC 6834, and the metadata lists no later RFC replacing it. The text restricts its use to trusted, closed deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LISP encapsulates packets using mappings from Endpoint IDs (EIDs) to Routing Locators (RLOCs). Map-Versioning associates a version number with each such mapping and carries it in the LISP-specific header. When a mapping changes, such as when RLOCs are added or removed or their priority or weight changes, it gets a new version number.

Encapsulated packets carry the version numbers of both mappings used to pick the outer source and destination RLOCs. That lets the receiving Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) check whether the sender's Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) is using the latest mapping for the destination, and whether the ETR's own cached mapping for the source is current.

The mechanism is transparent to routers that do not support it. The document obsoletes RFC 6834, the earlier experimental specification, and builds on RFC 9300 and RFC 9301.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep an address book. A version number on each entry lets them see quickly if their copy is old.

sections.title: Where the Version Numbers Go
sections.content:
Setting the V bit in the LISP-specific header makes it carry a 12-bit Source Map-Version and a 12-bit Dest Map-Version. Not every encapsulated packet needs to carry versions.

Map Records in Map-Request, Map-Reply and Map-Register messages carry a 12-bit Map-Version Number as well. The RFC does not change how those messages work. The format is backward compatible, since routers without support simply ignore those bits. A Map-Server that receives a message with an unexpected version, such as an old one, MUST silently drop it and SHOULD log it.
sections.plainLanguage: The version number is written in two spots: on each package label and in the address book entry itself. Routers that do not understand it just ignore it.

sections.title: Version Numbers and the Null Map-Version
sections.content:
A Map-Version number is an unsigned 12-bit integer assigned per mapping, so different mappings are versioned independently. A newer version MUST be an increment of the older one. The number space is circular, using serial number arithmetic as in RFC 1982: half of the values count as newer than the current one and half as older. For example, with version 69, values 70 through 69 + 2048 are greater.

The initial version of a new mapping SHOULD be random, and MUST NOT be 0x000. That value is the Null Map-Version, meaning no version is associated. Packets for such a mapping MUST NOT carry versions (V-bit 0), and an ETR that receives V-bit packets for a null-versioned mapping MUST silently drop them. If an increment would land on zero, the version MUST be incremented by 2, so it becomes 1. ETRs MUST NOT automatically generate version numbers for mappings in their database.

A Source Map-Version of null means no version information is conveyed for the source site, so the ETR MUST NOT compare it with its cache. A Dest Map-Version equal to null is a protocol violation.
sections.plainLanguage: Versions count up like numbers on a clock face, and after the biggest number they wrap around. Zero is special and means no version at all.

sections.title: What an ETR Does With the Versions
sections.content:
On receiving a packet, the ETR checks the Dest Map-Version against its own database, where it is authoritative. If equal, nothing more is needed. If the packet's version is newer than the ETR's own, the packet carries an invalid number and MUST be silently dropped, with logging.

If the packet's version is older, the sender has a stale cache. The ETR MAY still process the packet, but the ITR MUST be told a newer mapping exists, using a Map-Request subject to the rate limits of RFC 9301. After 10 retries, Map-Requests go out every 30 seconds, and if the version is still not updated the ETR SHOULD drop packets with the stale version. If the previous mapping's Record TTL has already expired, old-version packets MUST be dropped right away without a Map-Request.

For the Source Map-Version, the check applies only if the ETR has a cache entry for the source EID. A newer version means the ETR's cached mapping is stale, so a Map-Request MUST be sent. An older version means the packet SHOULD be silently dropped. With no cache entry, the source version MUST be ignored.

To avoid an old number being mistaken for a new one in the circular space, the text suggests updating a mapping only when all active traffic uses the latest version, or waiting at least as long as the mapping TTL.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver compares the number on the envelope with its own. A bigger number is suspicious, a smaller number means the sender should refresh its copy, and the same number is fine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations of RFC 9300 and RFC 9301 apply. Map-Versioning MUST NOT be used over the public Internet and MUST only be used in trusted and closed deployments.

Attackers can try to trigger many Map-Requests by forging packets with random versions. Those requests are rate limited, and filtering packets with invalid versions before triggering a Map-Request helps against DoS, though the text says it might not be enough against a DDoS attack. Implementations are advised to guard against log exhaustion. The rules are deliberately conservative and drop packets in several cases, because control plane actions triggered by the data plane could be abused.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could scribble fake version numbers to make routers do extra work, so this is only for private networks where everyone is trusted.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
LISP needs several ETRs at one site to give identical mappings, and with versioning they must all return the same Map-Version too, otherwise extra control traffic, instability and disruption can result. Matching version numbers also make it easy to debug whether ETRs agree.

LISP has no synchronization mechanism, so xTRs must be configured consistently. In the example topology, both ITRs of Domain A must use the same value, otherwise the ETR in Domain B starts sending Map-Requests. If a synchronization mechanism appears later, Map-Versioning will use it automatically. The appendix covers unidirectional traffic, interworking with proxy routers and LISP-NAT, and RLOC shutdown or withdrawal. This document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: All the mailrooms at one site must write the same version number, or the other side gets confused and keeps asking questions.

fields.desc: Flag bits; V set to 1 means version numbers are carried.

fields.desc: Version of the mapping used to pick the source RLOC.

fields.desc: Version of the mapping used to pick the destination RLOC.
